rules.title: Linked User Requests
rules.description: User requests can be linked because they contain a unique identifier.
elicitation_questions: Is there an identifier (unique in system/session) or dataset?
Is there other data associated with that identifier?
Is there previous data with the same identifier to which new data can be linked?
consequences: Unique identifiers facilitate the linking of new data items to a user profile, accumulating growing amounts of personal data associated with this profile. This can later lead to ‘Identifying’ threats.
examples: be linked?  Using an email address as an identifier enables the linking of all activities to the same individual, even across multiple services.
 An IP address can be used to link multiple visits to the same individual.
 All product views in a web shop are linked to the same user because they are logged in.
rules.additional_info: Linking is especially easy for authenticated users, as all requests in the same session are linked.

rules.title: Linkable User Requests
rules.description: User requests can be linked because they contain attributes that can be combined into quasi-identifiers.
elicitation_questions: Is there a set of attributes that can serve as an identifier?
Is there other data sent together with that quasi-identifier?
Is there existing data to link it to?
consequences: . . ) that together are unique to a websi
The use of quasi-identifiers enables the linking of new data items to a user profile to gather increasing amounts of personal data, even without unique identifiers.
examples:  A small set of locations can be used to uniquely link activity to a single user.
 A subset of attributes may be suﬃcient to uniquely link data to a particular individual.
 A browser fingerprint combines properties (OS, browser, display size,.
rules.additional_info: Many requests contain a lot of different properties that, when combined, are unique to an individual.

rules.title: Linking Through Distinguishable Patterns
rules.description: Patterns in the (meta)data contained in user requests can be used to link them to each other.
elicitation_questions: Is the data from different individuals distinguishable?
Is it possible to query data using distinguishable attributes?
consequences: When users are distinguishable from one another, user profiles can be constructed to collect growing amounts of personal data associated with each profile. This can later lead to ‘Identifying’ threats.
examples:  Unique timing patterns could be recognized to link the use of a service to the same user.
 Messages can be analyzed for patterns (e.g., writing style, timing) to link them to the same user.
rules.additional_info: Even data without clear attributes could contain patterns to allow distinguishing between different individuals.

rules.title: Linkable Dataset
rules.description: Stored personal data can be linked to individuals.
elicitation_questions: Is there a set of attributes that can serve as an identifier?
Is there other data sent together with that quasi-identifier?
Is there existing data to link it to?
consequences: The use of quasi-identifiers enables the linking of new data items to a user profile to gather increasing amounts of personal data, even without unique identifiers.
examples:  Fine-grained raw data is stored that enables linking specific entries to individuals.
 Querying the average salary with a strict set of criteria can reveal the salary of an individual employee.
 Patterns in a person’s writing style can be used to link multiple texts written by the same person.
rules.additional_info: Many requests contain a lot of different properties that, when combined, are unique to an individual.

rules.title: Profiling Users
rules.description: Users can be profiled by analyzing their data for patterns.
elicitation_questions: Are there patterns derivable from the data?
Can (new) personal data be inferred from the linked data points?
consequences: Deriving patterns from the data can facilitate the linking of data that was not intended to be linked.
Timing patterns of messages can be used to link requests to construct profiles.
examples:  By applying sentiment analysis to faces in pictures, the emotional state of an individual can be derived.
 The frequency of data exchanges from a health monitoring device allows an adversary to infer a patient’s medical condition.
rules.additional_info: The more data is collected and the more detailed it is, the easier it can become to discern patterns for linking.

rules.title: Identified User Requests
rules.description: The incoming user requests contain data that directly reveals the user identity.
elicitation_questions: Does data sent to the system (potentially) contain identity data?
consequences: Identified data can severely amplify the impact of a future data breach.
Depending on the context, the identity may reveal very sensitive attributes (e.g., health records).
examples:  An online service requests full name and address during the registration process.
 The username for a service contains identity data (e.g., “firstname.lastname”).
rules.additional_info: Users often need to provide identified data even when not essential for the functionality. Identified data requires stronger security measures.

rules.title: Identifiable User Requests
rules.description: The user can be identified because the data in their requests can be used to infer who they are.
elicitation_questions: Are requests or records suﬃciently unique to differentiate them from those of a specific individual?
consequences: Even without identity information, user actions or data may be very specific and unintentionally reveal the identity.
examples: those of a specific individual?  User search queries, such as looking up nearby businesses or info about a rare illness, can be highly specific and may lead to identification.
 A person’s consistent access at a particular time each week could link their visits even when they are not logged into their account.
rules.additional_info: The likelihood depends on how distinguishable an individual is from others.

rules.title: Identifiable Data Flows
rules.description: Data sent to the system is suﬃciently revealing to identify the user.
elicitation_questions: Is there free-form user provided data that is received or processed by the system?
Is data collected that may reveal the identifying information?
consequences: Inadvertently providing identifiable attributes in user-submitted data can lead to the unintentional identification of the individual.
examples:  When an individual shares detailed data (such as location, employer, device type, etc.) in a feedback form, the provided information may be revealing enough to uniquely identify that person.
rules.additional_info: The data subject is not necessarily the source of the provided data.

rules.title: Identifiers In Data Requests
rules.description: Communication contains (quasi-)identifiers.
elicitation_questions: Is there a distinctive identifier used during interactions or when referring to an individual’s data?
Can multiple attributes be combined to create a unique reference to an individual or their data?
consequences: Pseudonyms facilitate the aggregation of data on the same individual (see linking). Storing a substantial amount of data increases the possibility of identifying the individual behind it.
examples: individual or their data?  The (re)use of an email address facilitates easy combination with other data, leading to the identification of the individual.
 IP addresses in communication can be used to uniquely identify an individual.
 Browser fingerprinting entails the combination of various properties to create a unique identifier, serving as a pseudonym for the user.
rules.additional_info: Identifying individuals through identifiers is easy when these identifiers are reused across multiple services or in publicly available data.

rules.title: Identifiable Dataset
rules.description: Stored data can be used to identify individuals.
elicitation_questions: Can multiple attributes be combined to create a unique reference to an individual or their data?
Is there a distinctive identifier used during interactions or when referring to an individual’s data?
consequences: Pseudonyms facilitate the aggregation of data on the same individual (see linking). Storing a substantial amount of data increases the possibility of identifying the individual behind it.
examples: referring to an individual’s data?  A dataset removes names and reduces addresses to cities.
Nevertheless, a combination of various attributes (city, birth date, language preference, etc.) could still be adequate to identify individuals.
rules.additional_info: Identifying individuals through identifiers is easy when these identifiers are reused across multiple services or in publicly available data.

rules.title: Non-Repudiation Of Service Usage
rules.description: Users cannot deny having used a service because of authentication or logged access.
elicitation_questions: Does the system record data affecting deniability?
Does the data itself impact deniability claims?
consequences: Identity information can magnify the impact.
Depending on the context (e.g., medical, whistleblower), this can have a large impact on the data subject.
examples:  An account with a corporate email address eliminates the employee’s deniability of having used that service.
 System administrators can access log files linking an entry in an internal complaint system to the individual employee.
rules.additional_info: If deniability is required, do not store the data at all or remove any attributable data. Avoid credentials with identity information.

rules.title: Non-Repudiation Of Sending
rules.description: Users cannot deny having sent a message.
elicitation_questions: Is the data digitally signed?
Which keys are used for signing? Who has access to these keys to verify signatures?
consequences: Signatures provide strong non- repudiation, as they can also be verified by third parties.
Append-only storage systems make it impossible for the data subject to later remove their personal data.
examples: signatures?  A digitally signed email prevents the user from later denying having written the message.
 A common spam countermeasure (DKIM) involves signing outgoing emails, this prevents users from denying the authenticity of leaked or stolen emails.
rules.additional_info: Signed data applies not only to messages, but also to documents, requests, etc.

rules.title: Non-Repudiation Of Receipt
rules.description: Users cannot deny having received a message.
elicitation_questions: Do (passive) interactions with the system (e.g., receiving a message) have side-effects (e.g., trigger transmissions, logging)?
Is deniability of receipt a desired feature for the system?
consequences: Some actions may trigger side- effects that impact deniability claims regarding those actions.
examples:  Read notifications serve as evidence that the user has opened/read the message.
 An individual’s browser history may be used to substantiate claims about their online activities.
 Actions can be logged as evidence.
rules.additional_info: These side-effects often happen implicitly or without user intervention.

rules.title: Non-Repudiation Of Storage
rules.description: Users cannot deny claims about data stored in non-repudiable storage.
elicitation_questions: Is the data digitally signed?
Which keys are used for signing? Who has access to these keys to verify signatures?
consequences: Signatures provide strong non- repudiation, as they can also be verified by third parties.
Append-only storage systems make it impossible for the data subject to later remove their personal data.
examples: signatures?  Data stored on a blockchain cannot be modified, eliminating the deniability of claims related to this data.
rules.additional_info: Signed data applies not only to messages, but also to documents, requests, etc.

rules.title: Non-Repudiation Of Hidden Data Or Metadata
rules.description: Hidden or metadata in a document prevent users from denying claims associated with it.
elicitation_questions: Does stored or transmitted data have associated metadata?
Are there embedded data or hidden patterns in the data or transmissions?
Does this data lead to undesirable deniability issues?
consequences: The unintentional inclusion of metadata with data or transmissions may impact deniability claims.
Hidden/embedded data can prevent a user from denying claims about the data.
examples:  Author or revision metadata in documents prevents deniability.
 Data watermarked with hidden artifacts (uniquely linked to a person) can be used to track the person revealing or disclosing the data afterwards.
 Remote resources (e.g.
image in email) are automatically loaded to track the user opening it.
rules.additional_info: This is also used as an explicit countermeasure to prevent people from sharing data.

rules.title: Detectable Users
rules.description: Inferring the existence of a user from the system’s response.
elicitation_questions: Does the system show status messages (informational, warnings, errors) when retrieving data?
Are the status messages distinct when an item (a file, user, . . . ) does not exist compared to not having access rights?
consequences: Being able to detect the existence of certain items can be a stepping stone to security threats.
Simply knowing the existence of data may be suﬃcient to infer sensitive information.
examples: exist compared to not having access rights?  A ‘wrong password’ error message reveals the existence of the account.
 A firewall responding with ‘port closed’ reveals the existence of a device at the IP address.
rules.additional_info: Prevent information leakage by not revealing the existence of items in system responses.

rules.title: Detectable Service Usage
rules.description: Detecting communication between a service and its users.
elicitation_questions: Can the communication be observed?
Can information be inferred from the observed communications?
consequences: In sensitive contexts (medical, whistleblower) detecting service usage may have a severe impact on the user.
examples:  Observing communication with a service to infer that a person is a user (e.g., adult website).
 Communication with a telemedicine service implies the user is a patient.
 Participation in the Tor network can be determined by observing traﬃc.
rules.additional_info: Services like Tor conceal the destination but the utilization of Tor can still be detected.

rules.title: Detectable Events
rules.description: Detecting side effects or communications triggered by application events.
elicitation_questions: Do actions in the system have side effects (e.g., saving a file, writing to a log, triggering other transmissions)?
Are these side effects observable?
consequences: Sensitive information may be deduced from observed side effects, such as communication.
examples:  Log files on a shared system reveal applications used or actions taken by other users.
 Deleted applications may leave behind traces (configuration, temporary files).
 When steganography is used to hide data, the increased file size may still indicate the existence of that hidden data.
rules.additional_info: Dummy traﬃc can be used to conceal actual events.

rules.title: Detectable Records
rules.description: Detecting the existence of records in a system.
elicitation_questions: Does the system show status messages (informational, warnings, errors) when retrieving data?
Are the status messages distinct when an item (a file, user, . . . ) does not exist compared to not having access rights?
consequences: Being able to detect the existence of certain items can be a stepping stone to security threats.
Simply knowing the existence of data may be suﬃcient to infer sensitive information.
examples: exist compared to not having access rights?  An error message stating ‘insuﬃcient access rights’ may inadvertently leak the existence of a specific record.
 An error message stating ‘address already registered’ when subscribing to a political newsletter reveals a current member.
rules.additional_info: Prevent information leakage by not revealing the existence of items in system responses.

rules.title: Excessively Sensitive Data Collected
rules.description: The system acquires more sensitive or finegrained data than strictly necessary for its functionality.
elicitation_questions: Is the data more sensitive than strictly necessary?
Is the data more fine-grained than strictly necessary?
Does the data encoding include additional (meta)data?
consequences: Processing excessively sensitive data amplifies the impact of a potential data breach, thereby increasing the consequences for the affected individuals.
examples:  Tracking a patient’s weight is pertinent for dieting apps but not for a contact tracing application.
 A smart meter shares realtime measurements rather than the aggregated consumption.
 A camera application on a smartphone does not necessarily need to record the picture’s location.
rules.additional_info: When designing the system, assess whether all the data is genuinely necessary for providing the system’s functionality.

rules.title: Excessive Amount Of Data Collected
rules.description: The system acquires more data than strictly needed for its functionality.
elicitation_questions: Is the amount of collected data necessary for the correct functioning of the system?
Is the processing frequency necessary?
Are there more data subjects involved than necessary?
consequences: Regular data collection results in an increased dataset, potentially giving rise to additional privacy threats, such as data mining for patterns.
examples:  A generic service that is not age-restricted should not request a user’s age.
 Recording patient weight on a weekly or monthly basis may suﬃce; collecting such information every half hour is unnecessary.
 Posts on social networks frequently include personal data about other individuals.
rules.additional_info: Evaluate whether regular data collection is necessary for the system’s functionality.

rules.title: Unnecessary Data Analysis
rules.description: Data is further processed, analyzed, or enriched in a way that is not strictly necessary for the functionality.
elicitation_questions: Is the data enrichment/analysis necessary for the system’s functionality?
consequences: Processing the data can be used to learn additional sensitive information.
examples:  A camera application on a smartphone does not need to perform face-based recognition or emotion detection.
 Analyzing a user’s blog posts for language proficiency is unnecessary for blogging functionality.
 User profiles accumulate unnecessary details over time, tracking a broad range of actions or service usage that is not essential for the provided functionality.
rules.additional_info: Evaluate which types of personal data processing are necessary for providing the system’s functionality.

rules.title: Unnecessary Data Retention
rules.description: Data is stored for longer than needed.
elicitation_questions: Is the data stored for longer time than necessary?
consequences: Storing data longer than needed serves no further purpose and increases the impact of a data breach.
examples:  Retaining the email addresses of newsletter subscribers long after they have unsubscribed.
rules.additional_info: Evaluate your storage policies. Consider how long you store personal data and whether you have a process to remove data you no longer need.

rules.title: Overexposure Of Personal Data
rules.description: Personal data is shared with more services or external parties than necessary.
elicitation_questions: Is the data necessary for the recipient?
Are there more parties involved than necessary?
How accessible is the data (public/limited/private)?
consequences: Overexposure of personal data may lead to unintended consequences, as others could reuse the data for unforeseen purposes.
examples:  Location data from a navigation application is propagated to all the other applications (e.g., calendar, mail).
 Personal data is disclosed to other users of the service.
 In a medical application, while collecting patient weight data is deemed necessary, making such datasets publicly available would be unnecessary and harmful.
rules.additional_info: Carefully assess the necessity of sharing personal data and ensure that the involved parties genuinely require access to that data.

rules.title: Insufficient Transparency
rules.description: Data subjects are insuﬃciently informed about the collection and processing of their personal data.
elicitation_questions: Are data subjects insuﬃciently informed about the processing of personal data, including the purposes and methods of the processing involved?
consequences: Insuﬃcient transparency may lead to data subjects being unaware that their personal data is utilized for certain purposes, especially if those purposes are different from what was initially indicated.
examples: personal data, including the purposes and methods of the processing involved?  Data subjects are not aware of the identities of the third parties with whom their data will be shared.
 The privacy notice provided to the data subject was not presented in clear and plain language.
 Data subjects are unaware that traﬃc cameras collect not only number plates but also facial images.
rules.additional_info: Data subjects must also be informed on any ‘indirect’ data collection, i.e. from third parties.

rules.title: Insufficient Information When Sharing Data Of Others
rules.description: When sharing personal data of others, users are insuﬃciently informed about the further data processing.
elicitation_questions: If a user shares personal data of others, is it clear what, why, and how that data is further processed?
consequences: Users may not realize that they are unintentionally sharing personal data belonging to other individuals.
examples: that data is further processed?  A user posting a picture on social media may not be aware that others in the picture are automatically tagged with a facial recognition system.
 Using a DNA testing service can entail sharing medical information about family members.
 A service invites a user to share their address book to find contacts on a service.
rules.additional_info: While users are often informed about the consequences of sharing their own data, systems rarely inform them about the impact of sharing data of others.

rules.title: Insufficient Privacy Controls
rules.description: Data subjects have insuﬃcient controls to manage their preferences.
elicitation_questions: Does the system enable the data subject to configure which personal data is processed and for what purposes?
Can the data subject alter their preferences afterwards?
consequences: Appropriate control mechanisms are required to record data subject preferences and keep track of how the data may be further processed.
examples:  The data subject is unable to set appropriate preferences on which data is shared and why.
 The data subject is unable to set their consent preferences for the processing of personal data.
rules.additional_info: Privacy-friendly settings should be the default. Nudging can raise awareness and induce more privacy-preserving behavior.

rules.title: Insufficient Access
rules.description: Data subjects do not have access to their personal data.
elicitation_questions: Do data subjects lack the ability to access the personal data being collected, processed, stored, or disclosed about them?
consequences: Lack of access may violate the legal rights of data subjects.
examples: collected, processed, stored, or disclosed about them?  It is not possible for a data subject to request access, neither directly through the system nor indirectly through a helpdesk.
 The sensor data from a wearable is transmitted to a lifestyle tracking app, but the user cannot access statistics and information derived from their data.
rules.additional_info: The right to access is not always absolute. Limitations may exist depending on applicable laws (e.g., trade secrets, rights of other data subjects).

rules.title: Insufficient Rectification Or Erasure
rules.description: Data subjects cannot rectify or erase their personal data.
elicitation_questions: Do data subjects have the ability to correct or delete their personal data?
consequences: Data subjects have the right to rectify incorrect personal data or request the removal of data that is no longer relevant or needed.
examples: data?  The data subject is unable to correct their personal data.
 When a data subject deletes their social media account, the account is disabled, but the actual data is not erased.
 A data subject is unable to update their home address after relocating.
rules.additional_info: Rectification or erasure can also be performed indirectly (e.g., through a customer service ticket).

rules.title: Non-Compliance Of Processing With Applicable Regulations
rules.description: The processing of personal data by the system is not compliant with applicable privacy regulations.
elicitation_questions: Will the system be used in jurisdictions with specific rules for personal data processing (e.g., the EU)?
Does the system, or its processing activities, violate one or more rules in these applicable regulation(s)?
consequences: Non-compliance with local regulations may lead to hefty fines or other sanctions.
High-profile complaint cases or lawsuits may lead to negative media exposure and reputational damage.
examples: in these applicable regulation(s)?  The system processes information of EU citizens without a valid legal ground under GDPR.
 The system shares user information with third parties, violating ’Do Not Sell My Data’ rights under the CCPA.
rules.additional_info: Before processing any personal data, perform an assessment on the applicable regulations for your processing activities and system.

rules.title: Non-Adherence To Privacy Standards
rules.description: The system is not compliant with privacy standards and best practices.
elicitation_questions: Are there any (industry) specific privacy standards that are applicable to the system?
Does the system adequately implement the principles and controls outlined in these standards?
consequences: Non-adherence to industry standards and best practices makes it more diﬃcult to demonstrate compliance with applicable laws.
examples: outlined in these standards?  The system does not adhere to the best practices and principles outlined in the relevant ISO norms on data protection and privacy- by-design.
 Privacy risks are not classified and managed using a standardized methodology such as the NIST Privacy Framework.
rules.additional_info: Check whether there is industry-specific guidance on data processing for your sector (e.g., healthcare, manufacturing).

rules.title: Improper Data Lifecycle Management
rules.description: Data is not properly managed throughout its entire lifecycle within the system.
elicitation_questions: Is there a data lifecycle management policy defined for the data processed within the system?
Does the policy outline clear principles for each phase of the data lifecycle (creation, storage, sharing and usage, archival, and destruction)?
consequences: Inadequate or nonexistent data lifecycle management can result in a loss of overview of the data within the system and its maintenance, posing concerns not only for privacy and data protection but also security and availability.
examples: data lifecycle (creation, storage, sharing and usage, archival, and destruction)?  There is no clear policy or mechanism to enforce deletion of data that is no longer needed.
 The organizational roles and responsibilities surrounding data management in the system are not suﬃciently defined.
rules.additional_info: Data lifecycle management is a continuous process that must be consistently carried out as long as the system is designed, developed, and used.

rules.title: Insufficient Security Of Processing
rules.description: Data security measures and processes do not adhere to risk and security management best practices and standards.
elicitation_questions: Is there an established process to manage security risks and identify the required countermeasures?
Does the system incorporate the required countermeasures?
Are the countermeasures aligned with industry standards and best practices?
consequences: The security of the system plays a crucial role in safeguarding the privacy of individuals whose data is processed. Personal data breaches can result in significant fines and reputational damage.
examples: practices?  No security assessment was performed of the software.
 There are no processes in place to ensure software and services are kept up to date.
 The organization does not use appropriate access control mechanisms to limit access of employees to personal data.
rules.additional_info: Consider complementary methods like security threat modeling. Consider adhering to standards such as ISO27001 or the CIS Security Controls.
